stops.name: Étaples, landfall in France
stops.campa: Second Lieutenant Tolkien of the 11th Battalion, Lancashire Fusiliers, disembarks at the vast base camp of Étaples and moves up toward the front as battalion signalling officer. He carries in his kit the beginnings of his invented languages and a growing sheaf of poems. Ahead lies the greatest battle Britain has yet fought. He is twenty-four. The mud, the wire, the dead men's world of the trenches, the loyal batmen at his side, the roar and desolation, all of it is going down now into the deep, to surface later as the Dead Marshes, as Mordor, as the servant Sam who never leaves his master.
stops.quote: Junior officers were being killed off, a dozen a minute. Parting from my wife then . . . it was like a death.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, foreword to The Lord of the Rings

stops.name: La Boisselle, the death of Rob Gilson
stops.campa: On the first morning of the battle, walking forward as if on parade, Robert Quilter Gilson of the T.C.B.S. is killed near La Boisselle. Word reaches Tolkien days later. Something in the great design of the four seems to crack; he writes to Smith that a member of the immortal band has fallen and asks whether their fellowship, their high dream, can survive. Grief and doubt wrestle in him. The war is beginning to take, one by one, the friends who first believed in his vocation, and to press him toward the tales that will keep faith with the dead.
stops.quote: My chief impression is that something has gone crack. I feel just the same to both of you — nearer if anything and very much in need of you . . . but I don't feel a member of a little complete body now.
stops.quote_source: Tolkien to G. B. Smith, August 1916, quoted in Carpenter, Biography

stops.name: Ovillers and the Somme front, into the battle
stops.campa: In mid-July the battalion goes into the line before Ovillers, over ground already carpeted with the British dead of the first day. Tolkien lays and mends telephone wire under shellfire, sends runners and pigeons through the din, snatches sleep in dugouts. The 'animal horror' of trench warfare enters him. Here, amid the wreck of the immortal four, he grasps the truth his mythology will carry: that the small and overlooked, the private soldier, the plain hobbit, endure and matter more than the great. He survives assault after assault where thousands do not.
stops.quote: My 'Sam Gamgee' is indeed a reflexion of the English soldier, of the privates and batmen I knew in the 1914 war, and recognised as so far superior to myself.

stops.name: Beauval field hospital, struck down by trench fever
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of October, after four months in and out of the line, Tolkien falls sick with trench fever, the louse-borne illness that burns and racks him. Within a fortnight he is invalided back across the Channel to England. The fever that nearly kills him also saves him: it lifts him out of the meat-grinder that will devour so many who stay. Lying weak in the wards he begins, at last, to write down the great cycle of tales that has been forming in him: the mythology for England he had dreamed of with the T.C.B.S., now made urgent by the graves being dug behind him.

stops.name: Souastre, the death of G. B. Smith and the last charge to keep faith
stops.campa: Near Souastre, Geoffrey Bache Smith, the poet of the four, is struck by a shrapnel-burst as he walks along a road. Gangrene takes hold; on the third of December, at half past three in the morning, he dies. His last letter to Tolkien, written in expectation of death, lays a charge upon the survivor: that if he is scuppered, one of the great T.C.B.S. will still be left to say what they all dreamed. Of the immortal four, only Tolkien and Wiseman now remain. Tolkien edits and publishes Smith's poems, and takes up the dreamed work as a sacred trust: the mythology now a debt owed to the dead.
stops.quote: May you say the things I have tried to say long after I am not there to say them, if such be my lot. . . . Death can make us loathsome and helpless as individuals, but it cannot put an end to the immortal four!
stops.quote_source: G. B. Smith to Tolkien, 1916, quoted in Carpenter, Biography

stops.name: Great Haywood, The Cottage of Lost Play begun
stops.campa: Convalescent at Great Haywood in Staffordshire, where Edith has come to be near him, Tolkien takes up a battered exercise-book and writes across it in his own invented script the title The Book of Lost Tales. On the twelfth of February he begins the first tale, The Cottage of Lost Play, in which the mariner Eriol comes over sea to the isle of the Elves and hears their histories. The great legendarium is born, not in a study but in a soldier's sick-leave, out of grief for the dead and love for the woman near him. The village where two rivers meet becomes, in the tales, the Elvish Tavrobel.
stops.quote: I have hardly written more than a chapter of the tale of Turambar . . . before some of the events have come true.
stops.quote_source: Tolkien on the Lost Tales in wartime, Letters foreword

stops.name: Roos, in Holderness: Edith dances in the hemlock glade
stops.campa: Posted to command an outpost of the Humber Garrison, Tolkien walks with Edith in a small wood at Roos, thick with white hemlock in flower. There, in a sunlit glade, Edith dances for him and sings. In that moment the deepest of all his tales is conceived: a mortal man, Beren, comes upon Lúthien Tinúviel, fairest of the Children of Ilúvatar, dancing among the hemlocks, and loves her, and dares death and the Iron Crown to win her. He is Beren; she is Lúthien; the story is theirs. It becomes, he says, the kernel of the whole mythology, and the names will one day be cut upon their single grave.
stops.quote: In those days her hair was raven, her skin clear, her eyes brighter than you have seen them, and she could sing — and dance. . . . But the story has gone crooked, and I am left, and I cannot plead before the inexorable Mandos.
stops.quote_source: Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 340 (to Christopher Tolkien, 11 July 1972)

stops.name: Kingston upon Hull, the Fall of Gondolin written on army paper
stops.campa: Still weak with fever and posted about the Humber garrison, Tolkien writes on the backs of army marching-music the first and grandest of the tales: The Fall of Gondolin. The hidden Elven-city of seven names is betrayed and stormed by Morgoth's dragons and Balrogs of fire and iron; Tuor leads the survivors down the secret way while the towers burn. It is a battle-tale written by a man just out of the greatest battle of the age: the Somme's engines of steel transfigured into the foes of the Elves. That autumn his first son is born; the maker of worlds becomes a father in the ruin of the old.

stops.name: University of Leeds, the young professor and the runes
stops.campa: Tolkien takes a post as Reader, then Professor, of English Language at Leeds, the youngest on the staff. With his colleague E. V. Gordon he edits Sir Gawain and the Green Knight and drills students in Old and Middle English and the Norse sagas. Here his private mythology grows alongside his scholarship, and here he perfects the invented writing-systems that clothe his languages: the flowing Tengwar, whose shapes are built from the very features of the sounds they carry, and the angular Cirth, the runes cut for stone and wood. Like Barbier's night-writing and Braille's raised dots, his letters are a made script, a alphabet dreamed whole by one mind.

stops.name: The Tengwar and the Cirth, the sub-created alphabets
stops.campa: In the fictional deeps of his world the letters have their own history: the Tengwar are devised by Fëanor of the Noldor in Valinor, refining the older Sarati of Rúmil, their shapes a rational system where each stroke and bow marks a feature of speech. The Cirth, the runes, are made by the Grey-elves of Beleriand and elaborated by Daeron of Doriath into the Angerthas; the Dwarves take them up to carve in stone. He writes his diaries and book-titles in these hands, a maker of scripts as much as of stories, whose runes face the atlas's ciphers, the fingertip alphabets of the blind, the knotted quipu.
stops.quote: The Tengwar and the Certar (Runes) . . . were both of Elvish origin.
stops.quote_source: The Lord of the Rings, Appendix E

stops.name: Quenya and Sindarin, the two tongues and their kindred
stops.campa: In his notebooks the invented languages ripen into two great kindred tongues, each with its own music: Quenya, high and Latin-Finnish, the speech of the Elves of the Blessed Realm; and Sindarin, supple and Welsh, the tongue of the Grey-elves of Middle-earth. He works out their common ancestor, their sound-shifts, their divergence down the ages, as a philologist reconstructs Proto-Germanic behind English and Gothic. No man before has built a language so deep for love alone. And because a tongue must be written, he gives them the Tengwar and the Cirth, a whole civilisation of speech and script sub-created by one mind, to stand beside the world's true alphabets.
stops.quote: Nobody believes me when I say that my long book is an attempt to create a world in which a form of language agreeable to my personal aesthetic might seem real.

stops.name: Pembroke College, Oxford: Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor
stops.campa: Elected Rawlinson and Bosworth Professor of Anglo-Saxon, Tolkien returns to Oxford with a fellowship at Pembroke College. For the next decades he lectures on Beowulf and the old poetry, opening his classes by declaiming its thunderous opening, Hwæt!, so that a hushed room hears the very voice of the ancestral North. His 1936 lecture on Beowulf, 'The Monsters and the Critics', changes forever how the poem is read, arguing that its dragon and its grief are the heart of the thing, not a flaw. In his study at Pembroke he will write, in the margins of his day-labour, both The Hobbit and the beginnings of the greater tale.
stops.quote: Hwæt! Wé Gárdena in géardagum, þéodcyninga þrym gefrúnon, hú ðá æþelingas ellen fremedon.
